extracted.intended_audience: researchers/authors preparing manuscripts for submission to journals or conferences (especially in machine learning and related fields)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for authors on how to prepare manuscripts and respond to peer review in an environment where some reviews are AI-assisted or fully AI-generated. Focuses on pre-submission checks, writing tactics to resist superficial review, and how to handle suspect reviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make the reviewer-facing ask obvious early
rubrics_metrics.description: Most important move: Make the reviewer-facing or editor-facing ask obvious early rather than burying it in prose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this page as a tool/template: state explicitly what you want reviewers/editors to notice or act on up front. Avoid long explanatory prose that buries the explicit request.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish AI-assisted vs AI-generated review
rubrics_metrics.description: AI-assisted human review: Faster drafting and clearer prose when a human still makes the judgment. AI-generated review: Generic structure, plausible summaries, cheap scale where an LLM performed the reading and evaluation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat AI-assisted reviews (human formed judgments, AI only helped draft language) differently from AI-generated reviews (AI performed the evaluation). Most journals permit AI assistance if the reviewer’s scientific evaluation is their own.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of AI-generated reviews
rubrics_metrics.description: AI can't do the things peer review exists to do: it can't catch what it doesn't know to look for, can't reliably tell whether an interpretation is actually right, and can't hold itself accountable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect AI-generated reviews to produce competent-sounding summaries but miss tacit, field-specific methodological issues, offer hedged/weak alternate explanations, and show no reputational accountability. These reviews may function like generic summaries with appended concerns rather than substantive critique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicators a review may be AI-generated
rubrics_metrics.description: AI-generated reviews typically show: generic praise or concern not referencing specific figures/tables/data; balanced hedging language that avoids commitment; unusual uniformity of sentence structure; suggestions that contradict specific content in the manuscript.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a review reads like it could apply to any paper in the field, lacks references to specific experimental details (e.g., Figure 3), or contains improbable contradictions or hallucinated citations, treat it as a red flag for AI-generation or shallow engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Checklist before trusting a review that changes your submission plan
rubrics_metrics.description: Before you trust a review that materially changes your submission plan, ask: Does the review engage with specific figures, tables, or experiments? Does it identify a concrete scientific risk rather than generic prose concerns? Would the same comments still make sense if pasted onto a different paper? Does the review show the kind of field-specific judgment a real reviewer would bring?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If answers are weak, treat the review as structural feedback rather than substantive scientific judgment. Use these questions to decide whether to act on reviewer suggestions or to seek further expert input.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to respond if you suspect an AI-generated review
rubrics_metrics.description: You have options: flag specific concerns to the editor (observations, not accusations); request editorial assessment; write a thorough point-by-point response anyway; don't accuse directly in the response letter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame communications to editors as quality questions rather than AI accusations. Document engagement with each comment in your response to give editors the basis for overriding weak reviews. Avoid publicly accusing reviewers in formal response letters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write papers to resist superficial review
rubrics_metrics.description: Make your key claims figure-specific and reference your own results in the discussion so claims are tied to data; anticipate reviewers who won't read carefully; ensure methods and statistics are defensible without requiring a reviewer to read the entire paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical tactics: explicitly say 'Our main finding is in Figure 3B'; link claims to specific data points by figure number; make methods/statistics self-contained and clearly justified. These steps make it harder for shallow reviews to mischaracterize your work and force reviewers to engage with the data.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to use AI tools vs human expert review
rubrics_metrics.description: Use AI tools when you need a fast structural check, language polish, or to screen for common reporting/statistical errors. Use human expert review when you need evaluation of whether conclusions follow from data, journal-fit judgment, experience-based methodology assessment, or novelty evaluation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat AI as complementary: good for formatting, flow, grammar, and first-pass error detection; insufficient for substantive scientific judgment or high-stakes decisions. Don't substitute human expert review with AI for domain-specific validation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journals' current use of AI (screening vs substantive review)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some journals use AI tools for screening, plagiarism checks, methodology flagging, and language quality, but not for substantive peer review decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that editorial pre-screening may use automated tools; however, final scientific judgment at most high-impact journals still rests with human reviewers. Expect AI to affect early-stage triage rather than replace expert evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy landscape and enforcement limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Public guidance focuses on human accountability and disclosure; some journals explicitly prohibit AI-generated reviews and require disclosure, but enforcement is difficult because detection tools are imperfect and editors cannot easily verify authorship of reviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand that disclosure policies create accountability pressure but are largely unenforceable in practice. Detection tools flag probabilistic outputs and can be outpaced by fluent LLMs; editorial models (e.g., eLife’s consulting step) may provide structural protection where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-submission expert review necessity
rubrics_metrics.description: Pre-submission expert judgment matters more when official peer review quality is unreliable: getting real expert feedback before submission is the only way to be sure feedback reflects genuine scientific judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely solely on the formal peer-review system to catch unresolved scope-fit, citation gaps, or methodological risks. Invest in human pre-submission review by domain experts to reduce the risk of weak or AI-generated reviews derailing the submission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical red flags editors/reviewers may act on
rubrics_metrics.description: Highly specialized technical reviews that show no familiarity with specific methodological details of your paper are a red flag; reviews that could apply to many papers in the field rather than yours indicate poor engagement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If editors are presented with such reviews, they may remove reviewers from pools or ask for additional assessments. Authors should flag these issues professionally and provide concrete examples of mismatch (e.g., reviewer comments addressing a different study design).
